elicitation_input.question: X entered into a lease agreement with Y for house. X builds a hot tub on the property but once his lease expires he tells Y he wants to remove the hot tub as he built it with his own money.Y argues that he is the owner of the hot tub by accession. Will Y's argument succeed in court?
elicitation_input.question_type: Question that describes a hypothetical scenario and asks a question based on this scenario

llm_generation.text:
Y’s argument will likely succeed **if the hot tub has become a fixture** attached to the house or land.

Under the doctrine of **accession**, a fixture installed by a tenant can become part of the landlord’s real property when it is sufficiently annexed to the land, particularly where:

- it is physically attached to the property;
- removal would damage the hot tub, house, or surrounding land;
- it was installed as a permanent improvement rather than a temporary item; and
- the circumstances show an intention that it remain with the property.

The fact that **X paid for the hot tub does not by itself give him the right to remove it**. Courts generally apply the fixture test—physical attachment, intended permanence, and the relationship of the parties. Because X is a tenant, courts often presume that an improvement permanently attached to the leased premises becomes the landlord’s property, especially when the lease has expired.

However, X may remove it if it is merely a **trade fixture** or a readily removable chattel—for example, a freestanding hot tub connected only by temporary plumbing and electricity, capable of removal without substantial damage. A tenant is normally entitled to remove trade fixtures before the lease ends, unless the lease provides otherwise, but must repair any resulting damage.

Thus, **Y will succeed if the hot tub is a permanent fixture; X may succeed only if it remains a removable chattel/trade fixture or if the lease expressly permits its removal**.
